source.passage:
The gate at my aunt's nursery sticks in August, and she has never oiled it. I got there at seven, before the sprinklers, and shoved it open with my shoulder. I had come only to cover the shifts of the man who quit on her Friday. There was no wage in it, and no pane of mine to pay for. School had nothing to do with the day, and neither of us mentioned selling. A gravel path ran from the gate to the greenhouse door.

A card hung over the register on a loop of twine: NOTHING GREEN LEAVES HERE TO DIE. I had lettered it myself that morning, word for word as she dictated; the card was two hours old, she has never written one out in her life, she was not joking when she gave me the words, and she did not go against it once all day.

At nine a woman came in with a fig tree in a black pot, brown to the stem, and no receipt. She talked for a long while. Odile carried the brown fig into the greenhouse to nurse and told her to come back in autumn: no money out of the till, no second tree, no soil and no advice, and the woman went home with her hands empty. Nothing alive gets thrown out of this shop, she said. We had not grown that fig ourselves and it made no difference to her; a receipt has never decided anything here, and neither has a story from a stranger, and I am not teaching anybody a lesson.

I latched the gate at six. At breakfast I had told my mother exactly what my aunt would do, and I had been unkind and wrong about her. By evening the person I was ashamed of was myself. She had not been wrong about any of it, and I understood every step of what she had done. It was not admiration I felt, and there was nothing in the day to laugh at.

source.passage:
Kellerman's yard closes for good on the first of September, and I spent the last week of August there with my uncle Teodor. The launch Marisol stood on blocks in the shed, out of the water for the first time in forty years. My grandfather built her; Teodor ran her to the island and back for half his life. By Monday every house on the lake had a use to propose for her; by Friday she had a new owner. The marina at Two Harbours sent a cheque, and on Friday he signed it over to the bank. The sailing club had asked in June to teach beginners in her; he said a gift clears no debt, and no beginner boarded her. He had pushed a knife into her garboard plank in June; it went in no quarter inch, and no rot showed along her keel. The islanders would take the county's new boat; the crossing, he said, was no longer his. Petrus rowed over to trade his skiff and outboard; Teodor, who could still slip her single-handed, said a swap brings no money through the gate.

The bank had carried the mortgage since the bad winter, and the sum owed had grown past what a season of repairs could earn. Every other use proposed that week ended at the same wall: pay in September, or the doors would not open again. “The yard outlasts any boat in it,” he said, “and I will not shut these doors to keep one hull in the family.”

The sale drew half the lake to the shed on Friday, and I carried chairs out for people I had never met. He never asked the registry to put her name back on the list. I was not relieved, I was not proud of him, and nothing in it struck me as funny. There would be no crossing to dread in January; I was angry with him all evening, and knew even then the anger was unfair, since the cheque was the yard's one chance.

adapted.passage:
Kellerman's boatyard closes for good on the first of September, and I spent the last week of August there with my uncle Teodor. His boat, the Marisol, sat on blocks in the shed, out of the water for the first time in forty years. My grandfather built her, and Teodor ran her to the island and back for half his life.

By Monday, every family on the lake had an idea for what to do with her. By Friday, she had a new owner. The sailing club had asked in June to use her for teaching beginners. "A gift pays no debt," he told them, and no beginner ever stepped aboard. Petrus rowed over to offer his small boat and motor in a trade. Teodor could still handle the Marisol by himself, and he said a trade brings no money through the gate. Back in June, he had pushed a knife into her planks near the keel. The blade would not sink in even a quarter inch, and there was no rot anywhere. In the end, the marina at Two Harbours sent a check, and he signed it over to the bank.

The bank had held a loan on the yard since the bad winter, and the amount owed had grown larger than a whole season of repairs could earn. Every other plan that week hit the same wall: pay in September, or the doors would never open again. "The yard will outlast any boat in it," he said. "I will not close these doors to keep one hull in the family."

The sale drew half the people on the lake to the shed on Friday, and I carried out chairs for strangers. I had argued against the sale all week. When a neighbor told me my uncle had done the brave thing, I walked away without a word. I was furious with him all evening. I kept bringing it up at dinner long after he had stopped answering, and my jaw stayed tight the whole night. Even then, I knew it was not fair to blame him. That check was the yard's only chance.

source.passage:
Marta Sandoval spent thirty years compiling the first dictionary of the dialect of the high mountain province, working at a kitchen table between teaching posts. What happened to those finished pages is still argued about in the valleys she recorded. No volume of her own was ever bound, and she never paid a printer anything at all. The university library asked twice for the manuscript, and she had still not answered when the slips left for the capital; nothing reached the library. A newspaper offered to print one letter of the alphabet a month, and she refused to let the work appear in parts. A compiler in the capital borrowed her slips for a summer, and eleven thousand of her entries stand in his national dictionary under his name. A publisher across the border wanted a translation, but nothing of hers appeared abroad in any language.

One market day a week for nineteen years she stood among the stalls asking sellers what they called things, certain that people speak most truly while haggling over goods. She began each market day with the same question, the old name for a measure of oil, and set down whatever the first stall told her. A word went onto a card the first time a seller said it, without waiting for a second mouth. Parish books and wills she never opened, holding that a word owes nothing to having once been written down. The village teachers offered to have their classes write to her, and she refused: a child's page reaches the post already corrected. She kept no correspondents in other villages, saying that one market draws twelve villages to it, so postbags were waste.

Her name appears nowhere in his three volumes, not even among the thanks. It is no comedy, and hardly a waste, since the words did survive; her stubbornness is not the point, and impatience would be misplaced. The feeling the story leaves is indignation on her behalf, at a theft nobody has yet called one.

source.passage: Sociable weaver birds of the Kalahari construct enormous communal nests, thatched masses that shelter dozens of breeding pairs for generations. Biologists long assumed these structures endure because cooperation benefits every resident more or less equally, each bird gaining warmth and safety from the collective. A recent model complicates that picture. It proposes that the colony is held together not by mutual benefit but by asymmetric coercion: dominant pairs monopolize the thermally stable central chambers and tolerate subordinates on the exposed periphery only because those peripheral birds absorb the brunt of predation and weather, effectively shielding the core. Cooperation, on this account, is a byproduct of exploitation rather than its foundation—an arrangement that looks communal from the outside but is sustained by the inability of the weak to claim the better rooms.

source.key: Peripheral birds that attempt to move toward the central chambers are aggressively driven back by dominant pairs.

source.passage: The 'resource curse'—the observation that nations rich in oil or minerals often grow more slowly than resource-poor peers—is frequently taken to show that natural wealth is economically corrosive in itself. Where accountable institutions predate a discovery, they find, windfalls are managed without any subsequent decline in growth. The curse, on this view, is not a property of the resource but a preexisting condition the resource exposes. What looks like wealth causing dysfunction is dysfunction determining how wealth is used.

source.key: A nation whose institutions were rated weak before an oil discovery continued to grow slowly even after the oil was depleted and the windfall had ended.

adapted.passage: Countries rich in oil or minerals often grow more slowly than countries without them. This pattern, called the "resource curse," is often taken to show that natural wealth harms an economy by itself. Some economists disagree. In their view, sudden resource wealth does not damage a country's institutions, such as its courts and government, if they were sound to begin with. Instead, the wealth tends to arrive in countries whose institutions were already weak. It just makes that weakness easier to see and better funded. Where honest, accountable institutions existed before a discovery, these economists found, growth did not drop afterward. On this view, the curse is not caused by the resource. It is an older problem that the resource exposes.
adapted.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the argument in the passage?
choices: In several countries, growth fell sharply in the years right after a big mineral find.
A country with weak institutions before it found oil still grew slowly even after the oil ran out.
Countries with strong institutions tend to make and sell more kinds of goods than countries that rely on one export.
Sudden resource wealth has been shown to weaken institutions in countries that were well run before a find.
adapted.key: A country with weak institutions before it found oil still grew slowly even after the oil ran out.

source.passage: The extravagant songs of many warblers are usually explained as honest signals: only vigorous males, the reasoning goes, can afford the metabolic expense of singing, so females who prefer elaborate songs secure superior mates. Kowalski's field data complicate this tidy account. Across nine seasons, males with the most complex repertoires sired offspring no more likely to survive than those of plain singers, and females paired with elaborate singers gained no measurable increase in reproductive success. Song complexity, Kowalski argues, is not being maintained by the benefits it confers on choosy females but by the simple absence of any penalty for producing it: once the trait arose, nothing selected against its elaboration. The distinction matters, because it reframes a supposed triumph of adaptive design as something closer to an evolutionary accident that natural selection has merely tolerated rather than actively favored.
source.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Kowalski's explanation for the persistence of song complexity?
choices: Females consistently approached recordings of complex songs more quickly than recordings of simple songs.
Males with elaborate repertoires suffered no higher rates of predation or exhaustion than males with simple repertoires.
In a closely related warbler species, average song complexity has declined steadily over the past century.
Males raised in isolation developed markedly simpler songs than males exposed to adult tutors.
source.key: Males with elaborate repertoires suffered no higher rates of predation or exhaustion than males with simple repertoires.

adapted.passage: Many warblers sing long, complicated songs. The usual explanation is that these songs are honest signals. Only strong, healthy males can afford the energy it takes to sing them, so females who choose fancy singers get better mates. Kowalski's field data challenge this idea. Over nine seasons, the chicks of males with the most complex songs were no more likely to survive than the chicks of plain singers. Females paired with fancy singers did not raise more young, either. Kowalski argues that complex song lasts not because it helps choosy females, but because nothing punishes males for producing it. Once the trait appeared, nothing worked against it.
adapted.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Kowalski's explanation?
choices: Females went to a speaker that played complex songs faster than to one that played simple songs, every time.
Males with complex songs were caught by predators or worn out no more often than males with simple songs.
In a closely related kind of warbler, songs have grown simpler and simpler over the last one hundred years.
Males raised alone developed much simpler songs than young males that heard adult birds singing.
adapted.key: Males with complex songs were caught by predators or worn out no more often than males with simple songs.
